title: The Golden Age of Grave Robbing: Stuff You Should Know Live in London
summary: Live recording at Union Chapel in London of Stuff You Should Know on the history of grave robbing, centered on the late eighteenth and early nineteenth century "Golden Age of Grave Robbing" in Britain and America. The hosts trace medical dissection from the four humors and Galen through the Murder Act of 1751, the anatomy-school demand for bodies, and the London Borough Gang led by Ben Crouch and Patrick Murphy. They cover American cases including Grandison Harris in Augusta, Georgia, and the 1788 New York Doctors' Riot. They describe grave protection methods (mort stones, mort houses, set guns, torpedoes), the murders of William Burke and William Hare in Edinburgh and the term "burking," and the Anatomy Act of 1832. The episode closes with a list of famous robbed graves: Charlie Chaplin, Abraham Lincoln, Gladys Hammond (guinea pig activists), and Joseph Haydn's skull.
topics: Stuff You Should Know live London

segments.title: Live show opening and introduction
segments.summary: Hosts promote their SF Sketch Fest show, greet the London audience at Union Chapel, and introduce the topic of grave robbing and its Golden Age.
topics: Stuff You Should Know live London

segments.title: Early medicine, the four humors, and Galen
segments.summary: Early medicine relied on the four humors and Galen's anatomy for centuries. Practitioners were barbers and surgeons. In 1540 King Henry VIII granted barbers and surgeons four bodies a year for dissection.

segments.title: Murder Act of 1751 and body supply
segments.summary: The Murder Act added dissection to the punishment for murder, adding thirty to forty bodies a year. Convicts could also choose transportation to America or Australia.

segments.title: Medical schools, the body loophole, and the black market
segments.summary: Medical schools required students to provide their own bodies. Since stealing a body was not legally theft if the clothes and valuables were returned, demand led to a criminal black market for corpses.

segments.title: London Borough Gang, Ben Crouch, and Patrick Murphy
segments.summary: The London Borough Gang was founded by Ben Crouch, a former Peninsular War veteran who worked at Guy's Hospital and later retired wealthy. Patrick Murphy led the gang next and was underhanded, including selling and re-stealing bodies and sabotaging rival anatomists. The Naked Man anecdote is recounted.

segments.title: Grandison Harris and American grave robbing
segments.summary: In Augusta, Georgia, the Medical College of Georgia used an enslaved man, Grandison Harris, who was taught to read to follow obituaries and supply cadavers. The hosts note that grave robbing of marginalized and enslaved people drew little white establishment concern.

segments.title: How grave robbers operated
segments.summary: Robbers dug at night with wooden shovels, dug only the top third to the casket, pried it open, and pulled the body out with a rope. They stripped the body and reburied the valuables. Some robbers memorized floral arrangements. Others posed as family to take bodies from poor rural families. Hospital indigent burial grounds were also raided.

segments.title: Basement bones, Craven Street, and London Hospital
segments.summary: Bones found in medical college basements and on Craven Street, the Benjamin Franklin house, are discussed as evidence of dissection supply. In 2006 about 262 burials and bodies with wired skeletons were found at London Hospital.

segments.title: New York Doctors' Riot
segments.summary: The Doctors' Riot in New York City involved a crowd of roughly five thousand after a boy reported an arm in a hospital window and a man's wife's grave was found disturbed. The riot lasted several days, about twenty people died, and rioters searched hospitals and the Medical College, where Alexander Hamilton reportedly tried to calm them. Dozens of anatomy riots occurred across the United States.

segments.title: Grave protection: mort stones, mortsafes, set guns, and torpedoes
segments.summary: Families protected graves with mort stones, mortsafes (iron cages and stone mausoleums), watchmen, set guns that fired when a trip wire was tripped, and grave torpedoes, which were early land mines. Graveyards became dangerous places with shootouts.

segments.title: Burke and Hare murders and the term burking
segments.summary: William Burke and William Hare, in Edinburgh, began selling bodies from a boarding house after a lodger died owing rent, and then murdered people for their bodies. They sold to Dr Robert Knox. Their victims included Daft Jamie. Hare turned King's witness and Burke was hanged, with the body dissected. The term burking came from their methods.

segments.title: Anatomy Act of 1832 and the public view of dissection
segments.summary: Thomas Wakefield, publisher of The Lancet, warned about anatomy murder. After the London Burke-style trio was caught, Parliament held hearings and passed the Anatomy Act of 1832, which allowed unclaimed bodies to be used for dissection. The hosts discuss its criticism for burdening the poor, and that over 57,000 bodies were donated to science in the UK between 1832 and 1932.

segments.title: Modern outsourcing of skeletons and the top five robbed graves intro
segments.summary: Modern anatomy skeletons are often made of bones from grave robbing in India. The hosts introduce a list of famous robbed graves.

segments.title: Charlie Chaplin and Abraham Lincoln grave robberies
segments.summary: Charlie Chaplin's body was stolen in March 1978 from his grave and held for ransom of four hundred thousand pounds; the thieves were caught after police tapped the phone and recovered the body about ten miles away. Abraham Lincoln's grave was targeted by robbers about eleven years after his death, but the body was not taken, and it was later moved to a bolted steel cage.

segments.title: Gladys Hammond and the New Church Guinea Pigs; Joseph Haydn's skull
segments.summary: Animal rights activists in 2004 dug up Gladys Hammond and held her body for ransom to stop her family's guinea pig breeding for research. Later, Joseph Haydn's skull was taken during the phrenology era, kept by a collector, and a fake skull was buried; two skulls are now said to be in his grave.

segments.title: Q and A and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts open the microphone for audience questions and close the show, noting the episode is from How Stuff Works.
